lesson.topicTitle: Structure and functions in living organisms

specAnchors.text: understand the sources, roles and effects of the following hormones: ADH, FSH and LH

primer.text: You already met insulin and adrenaline as chemical messengers. This note adds three more: ADH, the kidney's water valve; and the reproductive pair FSH and LH, which run the menstrual cycle from the pituitary gland. For each one, learn source, role and effect — the summary table's three columns are the exam's checklist.

modules.title: ADH: the water-content controller
modules.opening: ADH (antidiuretic hormone) comes from the pituitary gland and answers one question — how concentrated is the blood? Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus sense the solute level: too concentrated means more ADH, which makes the nephrons' collecting ducts leakier, so more water returns to the blood and the urine shrinks to a small, concentrated volume.
keyPoints: ADH is released by the pituitary gland and controls the water content of the blood.
Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus monitor how concentrated the blood solutes are.
Low blood water means more ADH, leakier collecting ducts and more water reabsorbed.
The result is a smaller volume of concentrated urine when water is scarce.
High blood water reverses everything — less ADH, less reabsorption, plentiful dilute urine.

low.restatement: Low water: hypothalamus senses it, pituitary sends ADH, ducts get leakier, blood reclaims water, urine shrinks and concentrates.
low.analogy: ADH is the tap handle on the kidney's drain — twist it shut when water is precious, open it wide when there is surplus.
low.examPointer: Chain the sequence in order — hypothalamus, pituitary, collecting duct, urine — chain marks are standard here.

medium.restatement: ADH's effect is a permeability change: the hormone alters collecting-duct water permeability, so reabsorption tracks the blood's osmotic state detected by hypothalamic osmoreceptors.
medium.analogy: Imagine adjustable sieves — the hormone sets how fine the mesh is, deciding how much water drains away.
medium.examPointer: Name the detecting cells (osmoreceptors) and the acting structure (collecting ducts) — both earn separate marks.

modules.title: FSH, LH and the menstrual cycle
sourceHeadings: Hormonal control of the menstrual cycle
The roles of FSH and LH
modules.opening: Four hormones steer the menstrual cycle: oestrogen and progesterone prepare and hold the uterus lining, while the pituitary's FSH and LH run the egg's timetable. FSH matures an egg in the ovary and switches on oestrogen release; once oestrogen peaks, LH surges, triggers ovulation, and sets progesterone flowing.
keyPoints: FSH leaves the pituitary gland and starts an egg maturing in the ovary.
FSH also prompts the ovaries to begin releasing oestrogen.
When oestrogen reaches its peak, the pituitary is stimulated to release LH.
LH causes ovulation and stimulates the ovary to produce progesterone.
Oestrogen rebuilds the uterus lining after menstruation; progesterone maintains it for possible pregnancy.

low.restatement: Pituitary signals (FSH then LH) drive the ovary: FSH matures the egg and starts oestrogen, LH pops the egg and starts progesterone.
low.analogy: FSH is the coach who trains the athlete (egg); LH is the starting gun that sends her out and hands the baton to progesterone.
low.examPointer: Keep the two pituitary hormones separate — FSH matures, LH releases; swapping them is the classic error.

medium.restatement: The cycle is a hormone relay: rising oestrogen from FSH-stimulated ovaries feeds back to trigger the LH surge, so ovulation follows the peak — each gland's output becomes the next gland's instruction.
medium.analogy: Like passing notes in class: each message tells the next sender when to write, and the timetable never stalls.
medium.examPointer: Anchor each hormone to a source — pituitary for FSH and LH, ovaries for oestrogen, corpus luteum for progesterone.

glossary.definition: Antidiuretic hormone from the pituitary gland that raises collecting-duct permeability so more water is reabsorbed.
Hypothalamus cells that detect the concentration of solutes in the blood.
Follicle-stimulating hormone from the pituitary that matures an egg and switches on oestrogen release.
Luteinising hormone from the pituitary that triggers ovulation and progesterone production.
